draft.title: Validity of sources
card: A valid source is authentic and accurate. Authentic means it is genuine and from who it claims to be from. Accurate means its facts are correct.
Check who made the source and their expertise. Ask whether they know the topic well, such as a statistician writing about data.
Check the purpose and the date. A source made to sell something may leave out facts. An old source may be out of date.
Check whether other evidence supports it. If other reliable sources report the same facts, the source is more likely to be valid.
draft.remember: Check who, why, when, and whether other evidence agrees.

a.q: Why does a student check whether other sources report the same facts?
opts: Other reliable sources back up the facts
Other sources show who made the original
Other sources show how old the original is
Other sources prove the purpose is neutral
a.why: If other reliable evidence supports the facts, they are more likely to be accurate. Who made a source and when are checked by looking at the source itself, which is why those options are tempting but wrong.

b.q: Leo is researching how many Australians own a pet. A pet food company's website says 9 in 10 homes have one. Which check is most useful for judging this claim?
opts: Whether a national statistics survey agrees
Whether the company has traded for many years
Whether the company repeats the claim often
b.why: A similar figure from an independent survey is other evidence that supports the claim. The company has a purpose, selling pet food, so its own pages repeating a claim do not test it. A good-looking website says little about accuracy.
b.clue: Look for evidence outside the company.

a.best: Other reliable sources back up the facts

b.best: Whether a national statistics survey agrees
